clue.text: Soccer pass splits the French in game

indicators.note: the pass cuts through the middle of the French article, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: le is the French masculine form of 'the'
a cross is a pass from the wing into the box, so 'a cross' gives these letters

explanation.surface: A footballer's cross divides the French team during a match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'splits' puts A CROSS inside LE. The definition 'game' is the field sport played with netted sticks.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacrosse is a team sport played with netted sticks, so it is an example of a game.

clue.text: Concealed the French wine

parts.note: la is the French feminine form of 'the'
tent is a deep red Spanish wine, used for Communion

explanation.surface: Someone hid the French wine away.
explanation.walkthrough: TENT is an old name for a dark red Spanish wine, a crossword favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: Something latent exists but is not yet visible or active, hidden from view.

clue.text: Prospect showing part of cathedral (but not the close)

indicators.note: the close is the end, so the final letter of the cathedral part is dropped

parts.note: the chancel is the part of a church near the altar, for clergy and choir

explanation.surface: A view of part of the cathedral, though not of its walled precinct.
explanation.walkthrough: A cathedral close is the enclosed ground around it, which the surface suggests; here 'close' means the end, so 'but not the close' drops the last letter of CHANCEL.
explanation.definitionFit: A chance is a possibility or likelihood of something happening, much like a prospect.

clue.text: Port can get you stoned

indicators.note: the letters of 'stoned' can be rearranged to give you another word

explanation.surface: A harbour town where you can get high.
explanation.walkthrough: 'can get you' rearranges STONED. Ostend is a Belgian ferry port on the North Sea coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Ostend is a Belgian seaside town with a harbour for ferries, so it is an example of a port.

clue.text: Chair fabric above leg is slack

indicators.note: in a down clue the fabric sits above the leg word, so it comes first

parts.note: scrim is a coarse open-weave cloth used in upholstery for chairs
the shank is the part of the leg between knee and ankle

explanation.surface: The cloth on a chair above its leg has gone loose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'above' sets the fabric first in this down answer. 'slack' looks like an adjective for loose cloth but is a verb, to shirk work, from British military slang.
explanation.definitionFit: To scrimshank is British military slang for shirking duty, so it means to slack off work.

clue.text: County reduced numbers of employees

explanation.surface: A county council cuts its headcount.
explanation.walkthrough: STAFFS is the usual short form of Staffordshire, an English county in the Midlands; 'reduced' says the county name is shortened.
explanation.definitionFit: Staffs is the standard abbreviation of Staffordshire, and staffs are the workforces of businesses, a plural noun.

clue.text: Inept wit, frivolous and dim

indicators.note: inept means clumsily done, so the letters of 'wit' are bungled into a new order

parts.note: light means frivolous, not serious

explanation.surface: Someone with clumsy, trivial humour and not much brain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inept' rearranges WIT into TWI. 'dim' looks like a description of the person, but it defines half-light.
explanation.definitionFit: Twilight is the faint half-light after sunset, so in a phrase like 'twilight hours' it means dim.

clue.text: Number of craft — large number, if all milling around

indicators.note: the churned letters go round the word for a large number
milling about means moving in a confused crowd, so the letters of 'if all' are mixed

parts.note: a lot is a large number

explanation.surface: A big fleet of boats, all of them milling about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'milling' rearranges IF ALL into FILLA, and 'around' puts it round LOT. 'craft' are boats here, not skills.
explanation.definitionFit: A flotilla is a fleet of small ships or boats, a group of vessels.

clue.text: Worker in NE involved with metals

indicators.note: the letters of NE get tangled up with those of 'metals', making one rearranged pool

explanation.surface: A labourer in the north-east of England working with metals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involved with' rearranges NE and METALS together. The north-east of England was a steel-making region, so the surface fits the scene.
explanation.definitionFit: A steelman is someone employed in making steel, a worker in the steel industry.

clue.text: shopping?

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'shopping?' only, lowercase with no opening words: it looks cut short and no scan, search or reprint gives the rest

clue.text: Receiver, East European, faced by Detective Inspector

parts.note: DI is the abbreviation for a Detective Inspector, a British police rank
a Pole comes from Poland in Eastern Europe

explanation.surface: An East European suspect is confronted by a police detective.
explanation.walkthrough: 'faced by' puts the police rank in front. 'Receiver' is not a telephone or a fence: it is a radio aerial.
explanation.definitionFit: A dipole is a simple aerial of two rods, used to pick up radio or television signals.

clue.text: Steal? Could be mean as the Artful Dodger?

parts.note: to nick is British slang for to steal

indicators.note: the letters of 'mean' could be arranged otherwise, signalling a rearrangement

explanation.surface: Is stealing what makes the Artful Dodger so mean?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Could be' rearranges MEAN into NAME. The Artful Dodger is the pickpocket in Dickens's Oliver Twist; his real name is Jack Dawkins, so 'the Artful Dodger' is an example of the definition, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Jack Dawkins is known by a descriptive alias, so the Artful Dodger is an instance of such a familiar substitute label.

clue.text: Top decoration secured by nail if loose

indicators.note: the letters of 'nail if' come loose and settle in a fresh order

explanation.surface: An ornament on top is fixed with a nail, in case it works loose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'loose' rearranges NAIL IF; 'secured by' only joins the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A finial is an ornament crowning a spire, gable or bedpost, the topmost decorative piece.

clue.text: It's Hell in gangland

explanation.surface: Life among organised criminals is sheer torment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's' only joins the two definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: In myth the realm of the dead lies below the earth, like Hades; the criminal fraternity is likewise called the realm beneath respectable society.

clue.text: Frosty in the country? Here's fur

indicators.note: the cold word sits inside the country's name

parts.note: China is the country here
chill means frosty, icy cold

explanation.surface: It is freezing out in the countryside, so here is a fur coat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts the cold word inside the nation. 'the country' looks like rural land, but it names a particular nation.
explanation.definitionFit: Chinchilla is the soft grey pelt of a small Andean rodent, prized in the fur trade.

clue.text: How observant

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'How observant' (8): no parse of these two words gives OBEDIENT beyond a loose definition, so it looks cut short, and no scan, search or reprint gives the rest

clue.text: Accepting or taking office

explanation.surface: Agreeing to terms, or stepping into a post.
explanation.definitionFit: To accede is both to agree to a demand and to assume a throne or official position, so the participle covers consenting and entering a role.

clue.text: They're involved in board meetings

parts.note: a board meeting reads as a game of chess, played on a board, and the pieces are the ones involved

explanation.surface: Company directors attending boardroom sessions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'board meetings' suggests company directors, but the board is a chequered games board and the meetings are games.
explanation.definitionFit: The pieces of a chess set, kings, pawns and the rest, are what take part in a game on the board.

clue.text: Pay-off for gambler holding royal flush, say

indicators.note: the gambler wraps round the card word, holding it inside

parts.note: a backer is someone who bets money on a horse or team
a royal flush is an example of a poker hand

explanation.surface: A poker player holding the best possible cards collects his winnings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'holding' puts the cards inside the gambler. 'Pay-off' is not winnings but a bribe.
explanation.definitionFit: A backhander is a bribe slipped to someone, an illicit payment for a favour.

clue.text: Regarding speck in the far distance

parts.note: re means regarding, concerning, as in a business letter
a mote is a tiny speck of dust

explanation.surface: Looking at a dot far away on the horizon.
explanation.definitionFit: Remote means far away, distant in space, like something seen at the horizon.

clue.text: Sedative, one consumed after work

indicators.note: the piece for one plus consumed comes after the piece for work

parts.note: op is short for opus, a musical work
I is the Roman numeral for one
ate means consumed, eaten

explanation.surface: A tranquilliser taken once the day's labour is done.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after' puts the numeral and the eating word behind the musical work, short for opus.
explanation.definitionFit: An opiate is a drug derived from opium that dulls pain and induces sleep.

clue.text: Containers stuffed with the Spanish bread rolls

indicators.note: the bags are filled with the Spanish article, so it goes inside

parts.note: bags are containers
el is the Spanish masculine form of 'the'

explanation.surface: Bags packed with Spanish bread rolls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stuffed with' puts the Spanish article inside the containers.
explanation.definitionFit: Bagels are ring-shaped yeast rolls, boiled and then baked.

clue.text: Elegant ironic letter is enclosed

indicators.note: the letter word is shut inside the word for ironic

parts.note: dry humour is ironic and understated
ess is the spelt-out name of the letter S

explanation.surface: A stylish but sarcastic letter arrives sealed in an envelope.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is enclosed' puts the spelt-out name of the letter S inside the word for ironic.
explanation.definitionFit: Dressy describes clothes that are smart and formal, suited to a stylish occasion.

clue.text: Fancy tapes securing little flowering plant

indicators.note: the rearranged tapes hold the small word fast inside them
fancy is an adjective for something ornate and elaborate, so the letters of 'tapes' are rearranged

parts.note: wee is Scottish for little

explanation.surface: Decorative ribbons tie up a small plant in flower.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancy' rearranges the ribbons into STPEA, and 'securing' puts the Scottish word for little inside it after the S.
explanation.definitionFit: The sweet pea is a climbing annual of the legume family grown for its scented blooms.

clue.text: Riddle with arcane meaning — but that's not new

indicators.note: 'that's not new' says the letter for new is taken away
arcane means mysterious and obscure, so the letters of 'meaning' are scrambled

explanation.surface: A puzzle with an obscure solution, though it has been around a while.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arcane' rearranges MEANING, and 'not' removes N, the abbreviation for new, leaving six letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An enigma is a mystery or puzzling statement, something hard to work out.

clue.text: Make proud claim for Yorkshire town Henry ignored

indicators.note: the letter for Henry is left out of the town

parts.note: Harrogate is a spa town in North Yorkshire, England
H is the abbreviation for henry, the unit of inductance

explanation.surface: A Yorkshire town boasts it was overlooked by King Henry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ignored' drops H from HARROGATE, a spa town in North Yorkshire. H stands for henry, the SI unit of inductance.
explanation.definitionFit: To arrogate is to claim or seize something without right, presumptuously taking it as one's own.

clue.text: The last or first in the short list?

indicators.note: only the opening letter of the word 'the' is taken
short means the list word loses its final letter

parts.note: an agenda is a list of items for a meeting

explanation.surface: Is the end or the beginning of a shortlist what counts?
explanation.walkthrough: 'first in' takes T from the second 'the', and 'short' cuts the final A from AGENDA. 'first' looks like the opposite of 'last' in a definition, but it is the selection signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A tag end is the final remnant or leftover piece of something, its concluding bit.

clue.text: Leisure dissipated in Leeds on Sunday

indicators.note: dissipated means scattered, so the letters of 'in Leeds' are spread into a new order

explanation.surface: A Sunday spent wasting time in Leeds, a city in Yorkshire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dissipated' rearranges the first two words into IDLENES, and the abbreviation for Sunday follows it ('on').
explanation.definitionFit: Leisure is free time spent not working, a state of inactivity or ease.
